preamble: Dravet Syndrome  |  SCN1A-Related Developmental and Epileptic Encephalopathy  |  Severe Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy (SMEI)  (OMIM 607208)

questions.domain: First seizure onset within the first year of life (typically age 4–12 months)?
questions.question: Yes – Dravet syndrome characteristically presents with the first seizure between 4–12 months (median 5–8 months); onset before 6 months in >50% of cases; onset outside the first year is atypical and should prompt reconsideration

questions.domain: Normal psychomotor development prior to seizure onset?
questions.question: Yes – children with Dravet syndrome have normal developmental milestones before the first seizure; this pre-seizure normal period distinguishes Dravet from structural epilepsies, many metabolic encephalopathies, and congenital brain malformations

questions.domain: First seizure occurring in the context of fever or elevated body temperature?
questions.question: Yes – the inaugural seizure occurs in the context of fever in the majority of Dravet patients; fever from any cause (infection, vaccination, overheating) serves as the initial trigger; fever-triggered onset is the single most characteristic early feature

questions.domain: First febrile seizure following vaccination — particularly after DTP/DTaP administration?
questions.question: Yes – approximately 30–50% of first Dravet seizures follow vaccination (DTP/DTaP most commonly); this temporal association historically led to erroneous vaccine injury attribution; vaccination is a fever trigger, not a cause of Dravet syndrome

questions.domain: Prolonged first seizure — duration >15 minutes, or first seizure presenting as status epilepticus?
questions.question: Yes – prolonged hemiclonic seizures or febrile status epilepticus at the first presentation are characteristic of Dravet syndrome; hospitalization for the initial seizure event is extremely common; brief first febrile seizures are less typical

questions.domain: Male sex — Dravet syndrome has a slight male predominance (~60% male)?
questions.question: Yes – Dravet syndrome affects males slightly more commonly than females (approximately 60:40); this male predominance distinguishes it from PCDH19 epilepsy (its most important clinical mimic), which predominantly affects females

questions.domain: Recurrent prolonged febrile seizures or febrile status epilepticus across multiple febrile illnesses?
questions.question: Yes – recurrent prolonged febrile seizures with every subsequent febrile illness are a hallmark early feature of Dravet syndrome; the pattern of repeated prolonged febrile events over the first 1–2 years is highly characteristic and should trigger urgent evaluation

questions.domain: Hemiclonic seizures — unilateral clonic seizures alternating sides across different episodes?
questions.question: Yes – hemiclonic seizures (clonic movements confined to one side of the body, alternating between left and right across separate seizure events) are virtually pathognomonic for Dravet syndrome; this alternating laterality pattern is one of the most diagnostically specific features

questions.domain: Seizures exquisitely sensitive to even low-grade fever — temperature threshold as low as 38°C?
questions.question: Yes – temperature sensitivity is a defining feature of Dravet syndrome; seizures may be triggered by fevers as low as 38°C; warm bath water, hot weather, physical exertion, and emotional excitement can precipitate seizures through temperature elevation mechanisms

questions.domain: Seizure duration typically prolonged (>5 minutes) with recurring risk of status epilepticus?
questions.question: Yes – prolonged seizures lasting minutes to hours and true convulsive status epilepticus are hallmarks of Dravet syndrome throughout the disease course; status epilepticus is experienced by the majority of patients and is a major source of morbidity and emergency hospitalization

questions.domain: Development of multiple distinct seizure types after age 1–2 years?
questions.question: Yes – after the initial febrile-onset phase, Dravet syndrome evolves into a multi-seizure-type disorder including myoclonic, atypical absence, focal with/without bilateral spread, and tonic-clonic seizures; this evolution of seizure types is diagnostically important

questions.domain: Myoclonic seizures — brief, irregular, arrhythmic jerks of limbs or whole body?
questions.question: Yes – myoclonic seizures emerge after the first year in most patients; may range from subtle head nods and finger jerks to massive whole-body myoclonus; the emergence of myoclonus alongside febrile seizures was central to the original SMEI nomenclature

questions.domain: Atypical absence seizures — staring spells with variable onset/offset, possibly with automatisms or myoclonic components?
questions.question: Yes – atypical absence seizures (less well-defined clinically than typical childhood absences) occur in the majority of Dravet patients; may be subtle, brief, and easily missed without video EEG; they contribute to cognitive and behavioral burden

questions.domain: Nocturnal generalized tonic-clonic seizures (GTCS) occurring from sleep or awakening transitions?
questions.question: Yes – nocturnal GTCS are common in Dravet syndrome from the second year of life onward; occurring predominantly from NREM sleep or at sleep-wake transitions; nocturnal GTCS are a major SUDEP risk factor and source of sleep disruption

questions.domain: Pharmacoresistance — failure of multiple standard anti-seizure medications (ASMs)?
questions.question: Yes – medical refractoriness to multiple standard ASMs is a cardinal feature of Dravet syndrome; furthermore, sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine) WORSEN seizures in Dravet syndrome due to further Nav1.1 inhibition; treatment failure history is diagnostically informative

questions.domain: Hot bath or warm water exposure consistently triggering seizures?
questions.question: Yes – warm bath water is one of the most reliable and reproducible seizure triggers in Dravet syndrome; caregivers learn to use lukewarm or cool water; the hot bath trigger has very high specificity for Dravet syndrome and SCN1A-related epilepsies among all epilepsy syndromes

questions.domain: Physical exertion or exercise triggering seizures through temperature elevation?
questions.question: Yes – physical exertion and the associated rise in core body temperature is a reliable seizure trigger in Dravet syndrome; limits participation in physical activity and sport; cooling strategies (cooling vests, air-conditioned environments) are used prophylactically

questions.domain: Photosensitivity — flickering lights or visual stimuli triggering seizures or EEG discharges?
questions.question: Yes – photosensitivity (photic-induced EEG paroxysmal responses or clinical seizures) is present in approximately 40–50% of Dravet patients; more prominent in early childhood; photosensitive spectacles and screen-use modifications may be recommended

questions.domain: Pattern sensitivity — geometric patterns, stripes, or specific visual environments triggering symptoms?
questions.question: Yes – pattern sensitivity beyond general photosensitivity is present in a subset of Dravet patients; contributes to caregiver vigilance and avoidance behaviors around certain visual environments

questions.domain: Developmental plateau or regression following seizure onset — especially after first prolonged event?
questions.question: Yes – most children with Dravet syndrome have relatively normal development until seizure onset, then show developmental plateau or frank regression particularly after the first episode of febrile status epilepticus; regression often becomes clinically apparent between ages 2–5

questions.domain: Intellectual disability — mild to severe — confirmed on formal developmental or neuropsychological testing?
questions.question: Yes – intellectual disability is present in the vast majority of Dravet patients by school age; severity ranges from borderline to profound; correlates with total seizure burden, frequency of status epilepticus, and SCN1A variant class

questions.domain: Language delay — expressive language more severely impaired than receptive language?
questions.question: Yes – language delay is near-universal in Dravet syndrome; expressive language is disproportionately affected relative to receptive understanding; vocabulary acquisition is slow and some patients remain minimally verbal; augmentative communication is often beneficial

questions.domain: Hyperactivity, impulsivity, and attention difficulties consistent with ADHD features?
questions.question: Yes – ADHD-like features (impulsivity, hyperactivity, inattention) are extremely prevalent in Dravet syndrome; present in the majority; these features significantly complicate school performance and behavioral management alongside seizure control

questions.domain: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) features or formal ASD diagnosis?
questions.question: Yes – ASD or significant autistic features are reported in 15–30% of Dravet patients; social communication difficulties, restricted interests, and repetitive behaviors; may precede or emerge alongside developmental regression

questions.domain: Oppositional behavior, emotional dysregulation, or dysexecutive features?
questions.question: Yes – oppositional, stubborn, and emotionally dysregulated behavior is a characteristic part of the Dravet behavioral phenotype; likely intrinsic to SCN1A-related disruption of prefrontal inhibitory circuits; not solely secondary to frustration with disability

questions.domain: Anxiety, compulsive behaviors, or rigid adherence to routines?
questions.question: Yes – anxiety disorders and compulsive or ritualized behaviors are well-documented in Dravet syndrome; may manifest as food selectivity, rigid routines, separation anxiety, and obsessive-compulsive features; require behavioral and psychological management

questions.domain: Characteristic "crouched gait" — stooped posture, bent knees, wide base when walking?
questions.question: Yes – a distinctive crouched, stooped gait with flexed knees and a wide base is highly characteristic of older children and adults with Dravet syndrome; described as Parkinsonian-like or squatting in quality; a specific and underappreciated clinical sign in established Dravet syndrome

questions.domain: Unsteady or ataxic gait that is not fully explained by postictal state?
questions.question: Yes – cerebellar ataxia and persistent gait unsteadiness are documented as intrinsic features of Dravet syndrome, not solely postictal; progressive worsening of gait coordination occurs in some patients over adolescence and adulthood

questions.domain: Hypotonia — reduced muscle tone on neurological examination?
questions.question: Yes – hypotonia is present in the majority of Dravet patients by middle childhood; contributes to gait abnormality, postural instability, and fatigue; reflects progressive neuromotor involvement beyond the epilepsy itself

questions.domain: Elevated risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP) — among the highest risk of any epilepsy syndrome?
questions.question: Yes – SUDEP risk in Dravet syndrome is estimated at 1–2% per year (15–20× background epilepsy population risk); driven by postictal respiratory suppression and cardiac dysrhythmia from SCN1A disruption in autonomic and cardiac conduction neurons; SUDEP counseling is mandatory

questions.domain: Autonomic features during seizures — perioral cyanosis, pallor, diaphoresis, or pupillary changes?
questions.question: Yes – autonomic manifestations during seizures are common in Dravet syndrome including perioral cyanosis, pallor, diaphoresis, and pupillary abnormalities; reflect seizure propagation through autonomic circuits from widespread Nav1.1 dysfunction

questions.domain: Sleep disturbance — frequent night waking, difficulty initiating sleep, or nocturnal seizure-related arousals?
questions.question: Yes – sleep disturbance is nearly universal in Dravet syndrome; nocturnal seizures disrupt sleep architecture; insomnia, delayed sleep phase, and frequent night waking also occur independently; nighttime monitoring is essential for SUDEP prevention

questions.domain: EEG normal or non-specifically abnormal in the first year of life — early normal EEG does NOT exclude Dravet?
questions.question: Yes – the EEG is frequently normal or shows only non-specific slowing during the first year of Dravet syndrome; this is a critical diagnostic pitfall; a normal early EEG should not be used to exclude Dravet when the clinical history is suggestive

questions.domain: Generalized spike-wave or polyspike-wave discharges emerging after the first year?
questions.question: Yes – generalized or multifocal spike-wave and polyspike-wave discharges become evident on EEG after the first year of life; may initially appear only during drowsiness or sleep; progressive evolution of EEG abnormalities parallels clinical progression

questions.domain: Photoparoxysmal response — photic-induced generalized discharges on EEG with intermittent photic stimulation (IPS)?
questions.question: Yes – photoparoxysmal response to IPS is present in approximately 40–50% of Dravet patients; more common in early and middle childhood; EEG photosensitivity may be detected before clinical photosensitive seizures manifest

questions.domain: Multifocal independent epileptiform discharges from multiple cortical regions?
questions.question: Yes – multifocal independent spike foci (temporal, frontal, occipital, parietal) coexisting with generalized discharges are characteristic of Dravet syndrome EEG; reflects widespread cortical hyperexcitability from Nav1.1 haploinsufficiency in inhibitory interneurons

questions.domain: Brain MRI normal at disease onset (essential to exclude structural epilepsies)?
questions.question: Yes – brain MRI is typically normal in Dravet syndrome at presentation; MRI is essential to exclude structural causes (cortical dysplasia, tuberous sclerosis, hippocampal pathology); normal structural MRI in a febrile-onset refractory epilepsy should increase clinical suspicion for Dravet

questions.domain: Progressive hippocampal abnormalities or mild cerebral atrophy on serial MRI in older patients?
questions.question: Variable – serial MRI may show mild hippocampal signal changes, volume loss, or subtle cerebral atrophy in older Dravet patients with high cumulative seizure burden; these findings are not present at onset and are not required for diagnosis

questions.domain: De novo SCN1A pathogenic variant — no family history of Dravet syndrome?
questions.question: Yes – approximately 85–90% of Dravet-causing SCN1A variants arise de novo in the proband; negative family history is typical and does NOT reduce pre-test probability for Dravet; both parents should still undergo targeted testing when proband result is available

questions.domain: Family history of febrile seizures, febrile seizures plus (GEFS+), or milder SCN1A-related phenotype in a parent or relative?
questions.question: Yes – approximately 10–15% of Dravet SCN1A variants are inherited from a parent with GEFS+ or febrile seizures alone; SCN1A variants show highly variable expressivity; careful history of febrile seizures in all first-degree relatives is diagnostically essential

questions.domain: Pathogenic or likely pathogenic SCN1A variant identified on sequencing?
questions.question: Yes – a pathogenic SCN1A variant is identified in approximately 80–85% of clinically confirmed Dravet syndrome; SCN1A encodes the Nav1.1 voltage-gated sodium channel subunit expressed predominantly in inhibitory interneurons; haploinsufficiency → cortical hyperexcitability → Dravet phenotype

questions.domain: Truncating SCN1A variant — nonsense, frameshift, or canonical splice site mutation (loss-of-function)?
questions.question: Yes – truncating SCN1A variants (nonsense, frameshift, canonical splice site) produce loss-of-function (LOF) and are most strongly associated with Dravet syndrome; LOF of Nav1.1 in inhibitory interneurons disinhibits excitatory circuits; truncating variants predict the most severe phenotype

questions.domain: Missense SCN1A variant in a functionally critical domain (transmembrane segments S4–S6, voltage-sensing domain, pore region)?
questions.question: Yes – missense variants in functionally critical SCN1A domains are associated with Dravet syndrome; pathogenicity depends on variant location, conservation, and functional data; missense variants in less conserved linker regions may have uncertain significance and require careful interpretation

questions.domain: Large SCN1A deletion or duplication identified by chromosomal microarray or MLPA (when sequencing is negative)?
questions.question: Yes – approximately 3–5% of Dravet-causing SCN1A abnormalities are large intragenic deletions or exonic rearrangements not detectable by sequencing; chromosomal microarray or MLPA is required in high-probability clinical cases where point mutation sequencing is negative

questions.domain: PCDH19 variant excluded — PCDH19 epilepsy is the most important clinical mimic of Dravet syndrome?
questions.question: Yes (especially in females) – PCDH19 epilepsy closely mimics Dravet: cluster seizures in context of fever, social regression, and female predominance; distinguished by X-linked transmission affecting females; PCDH19 sequencing should be sent simultaneously with SCN1A in phenotypically appropriate female patients

questions.domain: No structural brain lesion on MRI — focal cortical dysplasia, tuberous sclerosis, and hippocampal pathology excluded?
questions.question: Yes – structural causes of febrile-onset refractory epilepsy must be excluded by high-quality brain MRI; focal cortical dysplasia, TSC, and other cortical malformations may present with fever-sensitive seizures and require different management

questions.domain: Lennox-Gastaut Syndrome excluded — not primarily tonic seizures with slow spike-wave (<2.5 Hz) EEG?
questions.question: Yes – LGS may co-occur with or evolve from Dravet but has distinct features: predominantly tonic seizures, slow spike-wave <2.5 Hz, structural or metabolic causes in many cases; Dravet has different EEG and earlier febrile onset

questions.domain: No glucose transporter deficiency (GLUT1) — CSF/plasma glucose ratio normal?
questions.question: Yes – GLUT1 deficiency can cause early-onset epilepsy with fever sensitivity; CSF glucose ratio <0.45 and low CSF lactate distinguish it; ketogenic diet is beneficial in GLUT1 (also used in Dravet); GLUT2/SLC2A1 sequencing if suspected

questions.domain: No pathogenic KCNT1 variant — malignant migrating focal seizures of infancy (MMFSI) excluded?
questions.question: Yes – KCNT1-related epilepsy (MMFSI) has fever sensitivity and refractory seizures but shows migratory focal seizure pattern on EEG; onset typically neonatal to early infancy; quinidine has treatment relevance; epilepsy gene panel distinguishes

sections.heading:
Clinical History: No additional cost (obtained during patient encounter and caregiver interview)
Clinical Assessment: $200–500 (formal developmental/neuropsychological evaluation; ADOS-2 for ASD features; Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales)
Clinical Exam: No additional cost (neurological and behavioral examination)
Medium: $500–1,500 (EEG with photic stimulation and sleep recording $500–1,000; prolonged/video EEG $800–1,500; metabolic laboratories including lactate, amino acids, organic acids $200–500)
Large: $500–5,000+ (SCN1A sequencing + deletion/duplication analysis by MLPA $500–2,000; PCDH19 sequencing $500–1,500; epilepsy gene panel if SCN1A negative $1,500–3,000; brain MRI with sedation $2,000–5,000)

Pathogenic SCN1A variant identified (25 points) — DEFINITIVE DIAGNOSIS
Hemiclonic seizures alternating sides across separate seizure events (10 points) — VIRTUALLY PATHOGNOMONIC SEIZURE TYPE
Fever / temperature sensitivity as reliable seizure trigger (10 points) — CARDINAL FEATURE OF DRAVET SYNDROME
Hot bath / warm water consistently triggering seizures (10 points) — HIGH SPECIFICITY TEMPERATURE TRIGGER
Recurrent prolonged febrile seizures or febrile status epilepticus (10 points) — HALLMARK EARLY DISEASE FEATURE
First seizure in first year of life in context of fever (10 points) — CRITICAL ONSET DEFINITION
Developmental plateau or regression after seizure onset (10 points) — KEY NEURODEVELOPMENTAL FEATURE
Truncating SCN1A variant — loss-of-function (8 points) — HIGHEST SEVERITY GENOTYPE CLASS
Multiple drug failure / pharmacoresistance (8 points) — CARDINAL CLINICAL BEHAVIOR IN ESTABLISHED DRAVET
Myoclonic seizures emerging after first year (8 points) — EVOLVING SEIZURE TYPE HALLMARK
Intellectual disability confirmed on formal testing (8 points) — MAJOR NEURODEVELOPMENTAL COMORBIDITY
Crouched gait — stooped posture with flexed knees (8 points) — CHARACTERISTIC MOTOR PHENOTYPE IN OLDER PATIENTS
Prolonged first seizure / first-event status epilepticus (8 points) — ALARM FEATURE AT ONSET

Phase 1 — Clinical Evaluation (No Cost):
  • Detailed seizure onset history: exact age, precipitant (fever, vaccination, bath, illness), semiology, duration, laterality
  • Map temperature sensitivity precisely: fever threshold, hot bath response, exercise tolerance, seasonal pattern
  • Developmental history: normal milestones before onset; document plateau or regression timeline post-onset
  • Complete seizure type inventory: hemiclonic, myoclonic, absence, nocturnal GTCS, focal features
  • Prior ASM trial history: specific medications, responses, and any medication-induced worsening (sodium channel blocker history crucial)
  • Family history: febrile seizures, GEFS+, epilepsy in any first- or second-degree relatives
  Potential: 60–80 points for $0 in a typical Dravet presentation

Phase 2 — EEG and Metabolic Screening ($200–1,500):
  • EEG with photic stimulation (IPS) and sleep recording — photoparoxysmal response, multifocal discharges, generalized spike-wave
  • Note: normal EEG in the first year does NOT exclude Dravet — repeat EEG if clinical suspicion high
  • Metabolic screening when indicated: plasma lactate, amino acids, urine organic acids (exclude mitochondrial, organic acidemia)
  • Fasting glucose and CSF/plasma glucose ratio if GLUT1 deficiency considered
  Additional: 10–25 points for $200–1,500

Phase 3 — Definitive Genetic Testing ($500–3,000):
  • Step 1: SCN1A sequencing + deletion/duplication analysis (MLPA or microarray) — detects ~85% of Dravet cases
  • In all female patients: send PCDH19 sequencing simultaneously with SCN1A (critical — PCDH19 epilepsy is the primary mimic)
  • Step 2: If SCN1A negative in high-probability case — comprehensive epilepsy gene panel (SCN1A, SCN2A, SCN8A, PCDH19, KCNT1, HCN1, GABRA1, GABRG2, CDKL5)
  • Brain MRI: high-quality 3T protocol to exclude structural causes; may be normal — normal MRI does not exclude Dravet
  • Parental testing: both parents should be tested for SCN1A variant when proband result available (10–15% are inherited)
  Additional: 25–45 points — crosses diagnostic threshold in the large majority of true Dravet cases

• SODIUM CHANNEL BLOCKERS ARE ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED — carbamazepine (Tegretol), phenytoin (Dilantin), lamotrigine (Lamictal), and oxcarbazepine WORSEN seizures in Dravet syndrome by further inhibiting Nav1.1 in inhibitory interneurons; administering these before diagnosis is confirmed can precipitate life-threatening seizure escalation
• FOUR KEY TREATMENT OPTIONS: (1) Epidiolex/cannabidiol — FDA approved 2018 (Jazz Pharmaceuticals); first specific approval for Dravet; (2) Fintepla/fenfluramine — FDA approved 2020 (UCB); reduces convulsive seizure frequency; (3) Diacomit/stiripentol — used in combination with clobazam; approved in EU/Canada, available under orphan drug in US; (4) Clobazam/Onfi — first-line benzodiazepine adjunct; valproic acid also used first-line
• EMERGING THERAPIES: Zorevunersen/STK-001 (Stoke Therapeutics) — antisense oligonucleotide upregulating SCN1A mRNA from the functional allele; in Phase 3 trials (EMPEROR study) as of 2025; ETX101 (Encoded Therapeutics) — AAV9-based gene regulation therapy targeting SCN1A expression in GABAergic interneurons; received FDA Breakthrough Therapy Designation early 2026
• VACCINATION — Dravet patients should continue to receive all standard vaccinations; the vaccine-induced fever is the trigger, not the vaccine itself; pre-vaccination protocol: antipyretics 30 minutes before vaccination, emergency benzodiazepine prescription available, observation period post-vaccination
• RESCUE MEDICATION — every Dravet family must have a prescribed emergency seizure protocol and adequate supply: intranasal midazolam (Nayzilam), buccal clonazepam, or rectal diazepam (Diastat) for seizures lasting >5 minutes; families should be trained in administration and when to call emergency services
• SUDEP PREVENTION — nocturnal supervision, seizure detection monitoring devices (mattress sensors, wearable monitors), safe sleep environment, and avoidance of prone sleeping position; SUDEP counseling must be documented and revisited annually
• HEAT MANAGEMENT is a clinical priority — air-conditioned home and school environments, cooling vests for physical activity, avoidance of hot baths (use lukewarm water), antipyretics at first sign of fever regardless of temperature level; these behavioral interventions significantly reduce seizure frequency
• SCN1A MOSAICISM — in approximately 1–3% of cases, the SCN1A pathogenic variant is somatic mosaic in the proband or a parent; standard clinical sequencing may miss low-level mosaicism; high-depth next-generation sequencing is required for detection; mosaic parents may have minimal symptoms while child has full Dravet
• KETOGENIC DIET — the classic ketogenic diet and modified Atkins diet are effective adjunctive treatments in Dravet syndrome with seizure reduction in 50–70% of patients; should be considered after two failed appropriate ASMs
Dravet Syndrome Disease Course, SCN1A Phenotypic Spectrum, and Key Differential Diagnoses

Disease Course — Temporal Evolution:
Year 1 (Febrile Phase): Prolonged hemiclonic or generalized febrile seizures; apparently normal development; EEG often normal; temperature the sole recognized trigger
Years 1–5 (Transitional/Worsening Phase): Multiple seizure types emerge (myoclonic, absence, nocturnal GTCS); developmental plateau or regression; pharmacoresistance established; EEG shows generalized and multifocal discharges; behavioral comorbidities appear
School Age: Intellectual disability clinically apparent; crouched gait develops; ADHD, ASD features, and behavioral challenges prominent; ongoing seizure burden; disrupted sleep; SUDEP risk ongoing
Adolescence and Adulthood: Convulsive seizure frequency often decreases somewhat; nonconvulsive seizures may persist; cognitive impairment and behavioral challenges continue; gait and motor features may worsen; supported living typically required in adulthood

SCN1A Phenotypic Spectrum (same gene, dramatically different severity):
  • Febrile Seizures (FS) — mildest; brief febrile seizures in childhood; complete resolution
  • Febrile Seizures Plus (GEFS+) — febrile and afebrile seizures persisting beyond age 6; outgrown in most; SCN1A variant in ~10%
  • Dravet Syndrome (SMEI) — most severe SCN1A phenotype; predominantly truncating/LOF variants; lifetime disease; developmental encephalopathy
  • Borderline SMEI (SMEB) — Dravet features without myoclonus; similar prognosis to Dravet

Key Differential Diagnoses:
  • PCDH19 Epilepsy — MOST IMPORTANT MIMIC; cluster febrile seizures; female predominance; social regression; X-linked; PCDH19 sequencing distinguishes; SCN1A negative
  • GEFS+ (SCN1A, GABRG2, GABRD) — milder spectrum; seizures outgrown in most; no developmental regression; family history common
  • Lennox-Gastaut Syndrome — overlapping refractory epilepsy but different onset; tonic seizures predominant; slow spike-wave (<2.5 Hz); structural causes more common
  • Doose Syndrome (MAE — Myoclonic-Atonic Epilepsy) — myoclonic-atonic ("drop") seizures; less temperature sensitivity; ESES on sleep EEG; often better prognosis
  • KCNT1-Related Epilepsy (MMFSI) — migratory focal seizures on EEG; very early neonatal to infantile onset; quinidine responsive in some; SCN1A negative
  • Angelman Syndrome — seizures with developmental regression but happy demeanor; 15q11.2-q13 methylation distinguishes
  • GLUT1 Deficiency — fever-sensitive seizures + movement disorder; low CSF glucose; responds to ketogenic diet; SLC2A1 sequencing

confidenceNote:
🔴  85–100 points: High Confidence — Dravet syndrome highly likely; proceed to SCN1A sequencing urgently; implement fever/seizure emergency plan immediately; avoid sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine)
🟡  40–84 points: Moderate Confidence — Dravet syndrome probable or possible; SCN1A sequencing (with MLPA) and PCDH19 sequencing (in females) indicated; epilepsy gene panel and video EEG recommended; clinical genetics/epileptology referral; avoid sodium channel blockers until diagnosis confirmed
🟢  <40 points: Low Confidence — Dravet syndrome less likely; broaden differential to PCDH19 epilepsy, structural epilepsy, GEFS+, Doose syndrome, or metabolic encephalopathy
